title: Every file upload 500s in the launch configuration: the unlimited storage quota overflows Postgres bigint
what: `unlimitedPlan()` substitutes `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (9007199254740991) for every int feature while BILLING_ENABLED=false. StorageService.put then computes `limitBytes = BigInt(limitMb) * 1024n * 1024n` = 9444732965739289378816 and passes it as a parameter to a raw `UPDATE tenants ... AND "storageUsedBytes" + $n <= $limitBytes`. Prisma binds it as int8; the value is ~1024x larger than the bigint maximum (9223372036854775807), so Postgres rejects the statement with SQLSTATE 22003. The throw is outside the try/catch (which only wraps `driver.put` at line 103), so it escapes as an unhandled PrismaClientKnownRequestError.
impact: With subscriptions off — the documented state for launch and for the 12-month free offer to the first five Greek libraries — NO tenant can upload a book cover, a member photo, a branding logo, a PDF attachment or a MARC file. Every attempt returns an opaque HTTP 500 with no actionable message. This is the first thing a librarian does after cataloguing a book. Turning billing ON is what makes it work, which is the exact opposite of what an operator would guess.
evidence:
RAN, end-to-end through the real services (RedisService + PlatformSettingsService + EffectivePlanService + StorageService, audit env, BILLING_ENABLED unset):
  billingEnabled() = false
  max_storage_mb effective limit = 9007199254740991
  UPLOAD FAILED: PrismaClientKnownRequestError | Raw query failed. Code: `22003`. Message: `value "9444732965739289378816" is out of range for type bigint`
The same probe with the Redis billing flag set to true uploaded fine (`UPLOAD OK -> covers/cmt5mkx9m6e5b01e495eb.png 70`). Confirmed at the SQL level too: `SELECT 9007199254740991::bigint * 1024 * 1024;` -> `ERROR: bigint out of range`.
Why this was never caught: apps/api/test/integration/setup.ts:8 does `process.env.BILLING_ENABLED ||= 'true';` — the ENTIRE integration suite runs in the opposite configuration from production, so no test ever exercises the unlimited-plan path.
fix: Clamp the unlimited sentinel to something a bigint can hold. Either make `UNLIMITED_INT` a value whose byte product still fits (e.g. 2**43 MB ≈ 8 PB) in effective-plan.service.ts:38, or — better — have StorageService treat the sentinel as 'no ceiling' and skip the `<=` predicate entirely: `const unlimited = limitMb >= Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER;` then run the UPDATE without the limit clause. Add an integration test that runs with BILLING_ENABLED=false and uploads a cover.

title: The documented "just re-run a failed import" recovery duplicates data, including double-charging patrons' fines
what: `requireRunnable` lets a `failed` batch be re-run and states "the engine commits each row independently and matches on the natural key, so re-running with skip/update is idempotent over rows a half-done commit already wrote". That is only true for rows that HAVE a natural key the engine looks up. `commitFine` performs a bare `fine.create` with no dedupe and `loanId` left NULL (so the `fines_one_outstanding_per_loan` partial unique index does not apply). `commitBook` only dedupes when `isbn13` is present. `commitMember` only dedupes when a memberNumber or email is present. `commitLoan` only blocks a duplicate ACTIVE loan; returned/lost loans re-insert freely. `commitReservation` relies on the `(bookId, memberId)` partial unique index, which only covers status queued/ready — canceled/expired holds re-insert freely.
impact: A 20,000-row import that fails at row 12,000 (worker OOM, tenant DB blip, deploy restart) leaves the librarian with exactly one documented action: re-run it. Doing so silently doubles every already-committed fine, every ISBN-less book, every closed loan, every member imported without a number, and every resolved hold. Patrons are billed twice with no audit trail distinguishing the duplicate; the catalogue gains phantom entries. There is no de-duplication tool and no undo. Bulk import is the onboarding path for every new library, so this hits customers on day one.
evidence:
RAN against the live tenant DB, driving the real ImportEngine twice over the same single-row payload (simulating the documented re-run):
  1) fine imported twice -> 2 rows, member owes 1000c (file said 500c)
  2) ISBN-less book imported twice -> 2 rows
  3) returned loan imported twice -> 2 rows
  4) number-less member imported twice -> 2 rows
  5) canceled hold imported twice -> 2 rows
All five ran with duplicateMode='skip', the safest setting.
fix: Make the re-run genuinely idempotent instead of asserting it. Cheapest correct fix: persist per-row progress — record `(batchId, rowNumber) -> entityId` in a control-plane table inside the same commit as the row, and have `processImportJob` skip rows already recorded when re-running the same batch. Until that exists, change `requireRunnable` to refuse re-running a batch whose `importedRows > 0` for entity kinds without a natural key (fine, loan, reservation, and book/member rows lacking the key), and change the UI copy from "re-run" to "contact support".

title: `books.isbn13` has no unique constraint, yet the import treats it as the natural key for skip/update
what: The import engine's dedupe contract ("duplicates matched on the entity's natural key are skipped, updated, or flagged") is implemented as `findFirst({ where: { isbn13, archivedAt: null } })` with nothing behind it — no unique index, and `BooksService.create` performs no ISBN check at all. So two book rows with the same ISBN-13 are trivially reachable: a librarian catalogues a title manually that also appears in the import file, or two writers race. Once duplicates exist, `findBookByIsbn` returns an arbitrary one, so `duplicateMode: 'update'` updates a coin-flip row and `resolveBook` attaches imported copies, loans and holds to a coin-flip row.
impact: The library's catalogue silently splits: the same book appears twice, its physical copies land under one entry and its holds under the other, and a re-import 'updates' whichever row Postgres happens to return first. Circulation counts, the OPAC and the reservation queue all diverge from reality. There is no merge tool, and the corruption is invisible until a patron cannot find a book that is on the shelf.
evidence:
RAN: four ImportEngine instances processing the same ISBN concurrently against the live tenant DB ->
  D) books with the SAME isbn13: 4  DUPLICATED
READ: schema.prisma:251 `@@index([isbn13])` (non-unique); books.service.ts create() writes `isbn13` with no lookup; the only ISBN constraint in migration SQL is `books_isbn13_shape` CHECK (digits-only), migration 20260526184041_init:486.
fix: Add `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX books_isbn13_unique_active ON books(isbn13) WHERE isbn13 IS NOT NULL AND "archivedAt" IS NULL;` (matching the barcode/member-number pattern already used at migration 20260526184041_init:470,475), and have `BooksService.create` and `ImportEngine.commitBook` translate the resulting P2002 into the existing 'duplicate' path. If the product genuinely wants two rows per ISBN (multiple editions), then the import must stop using ISBN as a natural key.

title: The import pipeline enforces `max_books` / `max_members` with an in-memory counter that ignores every other writer
what: Every other create path routes through `QuotaService.enforceWithinTx`, which takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock('quota:<tenant>:<feature>')` and counts inside the same transaction as the insert (apps/api/src/customization/quota.service.ts:63-65). The import engine does not participate in that lock domain at all: it snapshots the live count once in `init()`, resolves the limit once, and then decides per row from a private in-memory counter. The API process and the worker process therefore enforce the same ceiling against two different, non-communicating views. The interceptor's own header comment (quota.interceptor.ts:36-38) waves this off as an acceptable MVP race, but the codebase has since built the correct mechanism everywhere except here.
impact: A tenant exceeds its paid plan ceiling by exactly the number of manual creates that land during an import — unbounded in principle, and imports run for minutes. Under-billing is the mild reading; the sharp one is that today, with BILLING_ENABLED=false and the ceiling at MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, libraries will load catalogues of arbitrary size, and on the day billing flips on those tenants are silently over quota with no migration path and no warning surface.
evidence:
RAN against the live tenant DB with limit=10 and 5 books pre-seeded, then an ImportEngine committing 5 rows concurrently with 5 real `enforceWithinTx` creates:
  A) enforceWithinTx  limit=10 ok=10 rows=10  HELD      <- positive control, the lock works where it is used
  B) import || manual limit=10 rows=13  BREACHED by 3
The import engine never issued a `pg_advisory_xact_lock` (grep of import-engine.ts finds the lock only at line 651, for reservation queue positions).
fix: Have `commitBook` / `commitMember` call `QuotaService.enforceWithinTx` inside the same `$transaction` as the row insert, using the same `quota:<tenantId>:<featureKey>` lock key, and delete the `quotaUsed` / `quotaLimit` fields. Cost is one advisory lock per imported row on the same key the UI already uses, which serialises import rows against each other — acceptable, since imports are already single-threaded per worker.

title: Imported `ready` holds are permanently unfulfillable and never expire, freezing renewals on that book forever
what: `commitReservation` writes a status='ready' hold with `readyAt` set but `fulfilledByCopyId: null` and no copy flipped to 'reserved'. Three downstream invariants assume a ready hold owns a copy: LoansService.checkout refuses the pickup because `reservation.fulfilledByCopyId !== input.copyId` (loans.service.ts:266-270); ReservationsService.resolveReservation only frees a copy when `existing.fulfilledByCopyId` is set (reservations.service.ts:342-349); and the reservation-expiry sweep only matches `expiresAt: { lt: now }` (reservation-expiry.job.ts:92-95), which never fires when the import file carried no expiry date.
impact: The hold is immortal. It counts as a live hold for the `reservations_one_active_per_book_member` partial unique index, so that member can never place a new hold on that book; and LoansService.renew refuses every renewal of that book for every member while any queued/ready hold exists (loans.service.ts:623-631). Importing an existing library's hold list — the whole point of the reservation importer — permanently wedges renewals on each affected title, with no UI path to clear it other than a staff member finding and cancelling each hold by hand. The patron is also emailed "your hold is ready" for a book they cannot collect (member-notifications.job.ts:284-314 matches on status='ready' AND readyAt != null).
fix: In `commitReservation`, for status='ready' take the same `book:<bookId>` advisory lock the other paths use, claim an available copy with a CAS (`bookCopy.updateMany where status='available'`), set `fulfilledByCopyId` and default `expiresAt` to `now + holdPickupHours` when the file has none. If no copy is available, downgrade the row to 'queued' with a warning issue rather than writing an orphan ready hold.

title: `authors.sortName` has no unique constraint, so the "no duplicate authors" invariant the import advertises is unenforced
what: The import engine header states "authors are find-or-created by normalized name so a catalogue import doesn't spawn duplicate author rows", implemented as `findFirst({ where: { sortName } })` then `create`. Nothing backs it: there is no unique index on `sortName`, and `AuthorsService.create` does no lookup at all — a librarian can create the same author twice through the UI with no warning. Once two rows share a sortName, every later `findAuthorId` returns an arbitrary one.
impact: The author's bibliography splits across two rows permanently: browsing by author shows the name twice, each holding a subset of the books, and there is no merge tool. Since Greek names are accent-folded into `sortName`, near-identical spellings collapse into the same key and the split is invisible in the UI until a patron searches. Every subsequent import attaches new books to whichever duplicate `findFirst` happens to return.
evidence:
RAN: six ImportEngine instances committing one book each, all naming the same author 'Νίκος Καζαντζάκης' ->
  C) authors created for ONE name: 5  DUPLICATED
READ: authors.service.ts create() is a bare `client.author.create` with no sortName lookup; migration 20260526184041_init has no unique index on authors.
fix: Add `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX authors_sortname_unique_active ON authors("sortName") WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL;` and convert `findOrCreateAuthor` to an upsert on that key (catching P2002 and re-reading). Give `AuthorsService.create` the same lookup so the UI returns the existing author instead of a second row.

title: Member archive and hold placement use different lock domains, so a member can be archived while acquiring a live hold
what: `MembersService.archive` takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock('member:<id>')`, counts open loans AND active reservations inside that transaction, then archives — the comment claims this "serializes with the checkout path". It does, for loans: `LoansService.checkout` takes the same member lock and re-reads the member inside its transaction (loans.service.ts:229-238). `ReservationsService.place` does neither: it validates member status at line 110-122 OUTSIDE any transaction and its transaction takes only the `book:<id>` lock. The two paths never mutually exclude.
impact: Produces exactly the state `archive()` exists to prevent: an archived member holding a live hold. That hold still occupies the `reservations_one_active_per_book_member` slot and still blocks renewals of that book for every other member. When a copy is returned the queue promotes the archived member's hold to 'ready' and flips a physical copy to 'reserved' for someone who no longer exists — the copy is stranded off the shelf until staff notice and cancel the hold by hand, because checkout refuses archived members (loans.service.ts:162-166).
evidence:
RAN a deterministic interleave against the live tenant DB, replaying both services' exact transaction bodies:
  archive() sees activeLoans=0 activeReservations=0
  RESULT member.status=archived archivedAt=set queuedHolds=1
  RACE HIT: archived member holding a live hold
fix: In `ReservationsService.place`, take `pg_advisory_xact_lock('member:<memberId>')` alongside the existing `book:<bookId>` lock at the top of the transaction and re-read the member's status/archivedAt inside it, mirroring loans.service.ts:229-238. Acquire the two locks in a fixed order (member then book) in both services to avoid deadlock.

title: tenant-relocate lifts the source database's read-only fence before the control-plane cutover and cache bust, reopening the write-loss window it was added to close
what: The script fences the SOURCE database with `ALTER DATABASE ... SET default_transaction_read_only = on` precisely because, in its own words (lines 118-124), "admin/impersonation routes and background workers ... bypass the HTTP middleware" and their writes would be excluded from the snapshot and silently lost. It then lifts that fence at line 163-172 — BEFORE `tenant.dbUrl` is updated (line 174-179), before the TenantResolver cache is busted (line 202), and before the read_only system-mode window is closed (line 205). For the whole of that interval the tenant still resolves to the source database and the source is writable again.
impact: Any background sweep that fires in that window — fine accrual, reservation expiry, member notifications, all cron-driven and all bypassing the HTTP read_only middleware — writes to a database that is about to be abandoned. Those writes are already excluded from the pg_dump and are lost the moment the control plane flips. Silent, with no reconciliation step: a patron's fine or an expired hold simply vanishes. The same applies to any API process still holding a cached tenant client after the cutover.
evidence: READ scripts/tenant-relocate.ts. Execution order in the success path is: pg_dump (136) -> pg_restore (148) -> verifyDestination (155) -> unfenceSource (165) -> control-plane tenant.dbUrl update (176) -> bustResolverCache (202) -> closeEvent (205). The comment at 157-162 justifies the early unfence as "the source is no longer referenced" — but at line 165 the control plane still points every request at it.
fix: Move the `unfenceSource` call to after `closeEvent(modeEvent.id)` and after a drain interval equal to the TenantResolver cache TTL, so the DB-level fence is the last thing removed rather than the first. Keep the failure-path unfence at line 214 where it belongs.

title: Stripe subscription webhooks do multi-statement read-modify-write with no transaction, so concurrent deliveries lose updates
what: `syncStripeSubscription` reads the current subscription (582), decides `graceUntil` from what it read (630-637), then writes (614) and writes again (643) — four separate round-trips with no transaction and no row lock. The controller's Redis SETNX dedupes by event id only; two DIFFERENT events for the same tenant (Stripe fans events out in parallel, and the retry sweep re-drives never-processed rows) run fully concurrently. The stale-replay guard added at 601-612 compares `current_period_start`, which is identical for events within one billing period, so it does not order same-period events at all.
impact: Lost updates on a paying customer's subscription row: an `invoice.payment_succeeded` clearing `graceUntil` can be overwritten by a concurrently-processing `customer.subscription.updated` that captured the pre-payment state, leaving a paid tenant marked past_due — or the reverse, leaving a delinquent tenant with an open grace window. Because `EffectivePlanService` caches the resolved plan and clamps its TTL to `graceUntil`, a wrong value there directly gates or ungates features for real money.
evidence: READ. billing.service.ts:582 `const existing = await controlDb.subscription.findUnique(...)` and 614 `await controlDb.subscription.update(...)` are separate statements on the shared `controlDb` client with no `$transaction` wrapper and no `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. stripe-webhook.controller.ts:90-99 keys the SETNX on `event.id`, so it serialises retries of one event, never two distinct events. No handler in the dispatch switch (126-151) takes a per-tenant lock.
fix: Wrap each handler body in `controlDb.$transaction` and open it with `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('billing:' || tenantId, 0))` — the same pattern StaffService.create already uses on the control plane (staff.service.ts:73-75). Additionally store the Stripe event `created` timestamp on the subscription row and refuse any event older than the last applied one, which orders same-period events that the current `current_period_start` guard cannot.

title: `audit_log_retention_days` is sold and priced per plan but enforced nowhere; the tenant audit table grows without bound
what: The tenant schema states "Retention is governed by the tenant's plan (`audit_log_retention_days` feature) and enforced by a background job" and the plan seed prices the feature across five tiers (7 / 90 / 365 / 1095 / 3650 days, seed-data.ts:96-249). No such job exists in the registry, and no read path applies the limit either — `AuditService.list` (audit.service.ts:46) orders by `occurredAt` with no retention floor.
impact: Two problems, both real. Commercially, the retention ladder is a phantom differentiator: a Starter tenant sees and keeps the same unlimited history as an Enterprise one, so the pricing page misrepresents the product. Operationally, `audit_log` accumulates a row per meaningful change per tenant forever, in a per-tenant database with no pruning — for an active library that is the fastest-growing table in the schema, and it directly inflates every pg_dump, every relocate, and the DR restore time. It is also a GDPR data-minimisation exposure, since audit rows carry actor ids, IPs and user agents.
evidence: READ. `grep -rn audit_log_retention_days apps packages --include=*.ts` returns only the feature definition, the five seed values and a site copy reference — no consumer. apps/api/src/jobs/registry.ts registers nine jobs (support-session-expiry, reservation-pickup-expiry, stripe-webhook-retry, fine-accrual, export-file-cleanup, announcement-publish, book-metadata-refresh, member-notifications, storage-temp-cleanup); none prunes audit_log.
fix: Add an `audit-log-retention` job to the registry that, per active tenant, resolves `audit_log_retention_days` through EffectivePlanService and deletes `audit_log` rows older than the cutoff in bounded batches. Until it ships, either drop the feature from the pricing page or state that retention is currently unlimited for all plans.

title: Member-number generation runs outside the transaction that its comment claims serialises it, and gives up after three attempts
what: The comment at 221-225 says "The lock also serializes member-number assignment". It does not: `nextSequenceForYear(client, year)` is called at line 249 on the base client, before `createWithQuota` opens the transaction that takes the advisory lock. Concurrent creates therefore read the same max and collide on `members_member_number_unique_active`; the retry loop absorbs at most three collisions before surfacing an error. `nextSequenceForYear` also loads every member number for the year into memory (member-numbers.ts:42-45, `findMany` with no limit or aggregate) on every create.
impact: With four or more staff enrolling members simultaneously — a realistic school- or municipal-library enrolment day — a legitimate signup fails outright with a confusing 'A member with this number already exists' conflict, even though the librarian never typed a number. As the member table grows the full-scan per create also makes each retry slower, widening the collision window rather than narrowing it.
evidence: READ members.service.ts:249 `const seq = await nextSequenceForYear(client, year);` — outside the `client.$transaction` opened at line 227 inside `createWithQuota`. member-numbers.ts:9-12 acknowledges the race and prescribes a retry limit of 3; the loop at members.service.ts:247 uses `attempt < 3`.
fix: Move the `nextSequenceForYear` call inside `createWithQuota`'s transaction, after `enforceWithinTx` has taken the `quota:<tenant>:max_members` advisory lock — the number is then assigned under the same serialisation as the insert and the retry loop becomes dead code. Replace the `findMany` with `SELECT max(...)` over a substring, or add a per-year sequence row.

title: The nightly `storageUsedBytes` recompute that three code comments name as the drift backstop does not exist
what: `StorageService` keeps a cached byte counter on `tenants.storageUsedBytes` and, at three separate points, justifies best-effort error handling by deferring to a recompute: "run nightly in prod", "the nightly recompute (and `recomputeUsage` below) is the backstop", "a failure leaves the counter high until the nightly recompute". `recomputeUsage` is only reachable from `storage-demo.controller.ts:181`; the job registry contains `storage-temp-cleanup` but no recompute job.
impact: Every swallowed `releaseReservedBytes` failure (storage.service.ts:200-204 logs and continues) and every driver/DB divergence is permanent. Drift is one-directional — the counter only ever gets stuck high — so a tenant progressively loses usable storage until uploads start returning 402 with a usage figure that does not match what is on disk, and there is no operator command to fix it short of hitting a demo endpoint.
evidence: READ. `recomputeUsage` has exactly one non-test caller (storage-demo.controller.ts:181). apps/api/src/jobs/registry.ts registers nine jobs; none calls recomputeUsage. The three comments claiming a nightly recompute are at storage.service.ts:30, 113 and 189.
fix: Register a nightly `storage-usage-recompute` job that walks active tenants and calls `recomputeUsage`, or delete the three comments and make `releaseReservedBytes` failures loud instead of best-effort.

title: The reservation-expiry sweep stamps promotions with a clock captured before the loop, which can violate the `readyAt >= placedAt` CHECK
what: `const now = new Date()` is taken once per tenant at line 90, before the overdue set is read and before the per-reservation loop. Line 173 writes `readyAt: now` on the promoted hold. A hold placed after that instant but before its promotion has `placedAt > now`, and `reservations_ready_after_placed` (migration 20260526184041_init:521-522) requires `readyAt >= placedAt`.
impact: The whole promotion transaction aborts with a CHECK violation. The expired hold is not marked expired and the copy it was holding is not freed, so the sweep makes no progress on that book and the copy stays stranded in 'reserved' until the next run — which fails the same way if the queue head is still the newer hold. The service paths do this correctly (reservations.service.ts:501 and loans.service.ts:429 both take a fresh `new Date()` inside the transaction).
evidence: READ. reservation-expiry.job.ts:90 `const now = new Date();` sits above the `overdue` query at 92 and the `for (const r of overdue)` loop at 105; line 173 uses that same `now` for `readyAt`. Compare reservations.service.ts:501 `const now = new Date();` taken inside `promoteNextHoldInTx`.
fix: Take a fresh `const now = new Date()` inside the per-reservation transaction and use it for `readyAt` / `expiresAt`, keeping the outer `now` only for the `expiresAt < now` selection predicate.

title: Import member-number fallback can throw or mint an out-of-format number
what: After five failed attempts, `generateMemberNumber` returns `buildMemberNumber(year, Date.now() % 100000)`. When that modulo lands on 0 — a 1-in-100,000 chance per invocation — `buildMemberNumber` throws `Invalid sequence for member number: 0` because it rejects `sequence < 1`. For any value above 9999 the padStart is a no-op and the result is a five-digit number such as `M-2026-12345`, which is outside the documented `M-<YYYY>-<NNNN>` format (it still passes the DB regex, so it is written).
impact: Small but real: a large member import can die on a row with an unhelpful internal error, or silently mint member numbers in a shape the rest of the product (and the library's own printed cards) does not expect. Both only bite on a file large enough to exhaust five sequence attempts, which is exactly the migration workload this importer exists for.
evidence: READ. import-engine.ts:497 `return buildMemberNumber(year, Date.now() % 100000);`; member-numbers.ts:22-24 `if (!Number.isInteger(sequence) || sequence < 1) throw new Error(...)`; member-numbers.ts:25 pads to 4 with `padStart(4, '0')`, which does not truncate longer values.
fix: Replace the fallback with a collision-proof form that cannot be zero and cannot exceed the format, e.g. derive the sequence from `nextSequenceForYear` inside the same transaction as the insert (as recommended for data-integrity-11) and let P2002 drive a bounded retry, rather than guessing from the wall clock.

title: Verified sound: the advisory-lock quota strategy holds wherever `enforceWithinTx` is actually used
where: apps/api/src/customization/quota.service.ts:49-65; call sites in catalog/books.service.ts:201,357, members/members.service.ts:229,362, customization/collections.service.ts:111,212,289, customization/collection-records.service.ts:98, customization/field-definitions.service.ts:130, staff/staff.service.ts:73-109
what: Recorded so the gaps above are read in proportion. `enforceWithinTx` takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('quota:<tenant>:<feature>:<context>'))` as the first statement of the caller's transaction and counts inside it, so the count and the insert observe a serialised view per quota key. All ten call sites pass the transaction client, count within it, and insert within it. Un-archive paths (books 357, members 362, collections 212) correctly re-charge a seat, closing the archive-then-restore bypass. Control-plane `staff_seats` reimplements the same pattern against `controlDb` rather than skipping it.
impact: None — this is the control that the import pipeline (data-integrity-04) and the storage path bypass, and it is worth knowing it works before anyone rewrites it.
evidence:
RAN: 30 concurrent creates through the exact `enforceWithinTx` + `book.create` transaction body against the live tenant DB with limit=10 ->
  A) enforceWithinTx  limit=10 ok=10 rows=10  HELD
The 20 losers each received the 402 with feature/limit/used, and no 11th row was written.
fix: No change. Use this as the reference pattern when fixing data-integrity-04.
